text.S1: The wife of a rich man fell sick, and as she felt that her end was drawing near, she called her only daughter to her bedside and said, "Dear child, be good and pious, and then the good God will always protect thee, and I will look down on thee from heaven and be near thee." Thereupon she closed her eyes and departed.
text.S2: The wife of a rich man fell sick. When she felt that her life was comng to an end, she invited her only daughter to her bedside and said, “My beloved child, be good and faithful to God in prayers, so that the good Lord will always protect and be with you. As such he will look down on you from heaven.” There after she closed her eyes and passed on.

text.S1: When winter came the snow spread a white sheet over the grave, and when the spring sun had drawn it off again, the man had taken another wife. The woman had brought two daughters into the house with her, who were beautiful and fair of face, but vile and black of heart. Now began a bad time for the poor step-child. They took her pretty clothes away from her, put an old grey bed gown on her and gave her wooden shoes. Just look at the proud princess, how decked out she is!” they cried and led her into the kitchen.
text.S2: During winter, the snow spread a white sheet over the grave. When the spring sun had drawn it off again, the man had married another wife. The woman had brought two daughters with her into the house who were beautiful and looked humble in faces, yet they were starbon and merciless. Suffering now started for the poor step-daughter. They took away her pretty clothes from her and then she was dressed in an old grey cloth which was used as a bed cover, then they gave her a pair of a wooden shoes. “Just look at the proud princess, how nice she looks!” they shouted, mocked and led her into the kitchen.
text.T1: Maliha haa taha litwa layanduluka ni kukwahela busweu bwalona fa libita, mi lizazi la mbumbi halili omisa hape, muuna naase anyezi musali usili. Musali naa tisize bana bababeli ba basizana mwa ndu bane bali babande ni kubonahala kuluka kwa lifateho kono inge bali babamaswe ni situhu mwa lipilu. Cwale nako yetaata yakala mwa bupilo bwa mwanaa mwenda kumongo. Musizana bamu amuha libyana zahae ni kumuapesa lisila lakale leliseta lene liapeswanga fa mumbeta kona hape bamufa maheta a likota. “Hamubone mukwae yai kuhumusa, moo abonahalezi hande,” bahuweleza ni kumuseha kona bamulibisa mwa situngu.

text.S1: There she had to do hard work from morning till night, get up before daybreak, carry water, light fires, cook and wash. Besides this, the sisters did her every imaginable injury— they mocked her and emptied her peas and lentils into the ashes, so that she was forced to sit and pick them out again. In the evening when she had worked till she was weary she had no bed to go to, but had to sleep by the fireside in the ashes. And as on that account she always looked dusty and dirty, they called her Cinderella.
text.S2: There she was given hard manual work from morning till night. She got up before daybreak, fetched water, lit fires, cooked and washed. Besides that, the step sisters did her every imaginable injury. They mocked her and emptied her peas and lentils into the ashes so that she would be prompted to squat and pick them again. In the evening when she had worked till she was weary, there was no bed to sleep on but just to sleep by the hearth in the ashes. It was for that reason that she was always looking dusty and dirty and therefore, named her Cinderella.
text.T1: Naana ni kusebeza misebezi yebukiti kuzwa kakusasana konji kuyofita busihu. Azuha lizazi lisika pazula kale kuyonga mezi, kutumbula mulilo, kutateha lico ni kutapisa lika. Kwandaa zewo basizana bahabo bamwenda kumongo bamuholofaza ka kolofalo yesa nahanelwi ka kumunyefula ni kusululela manawa ahae ni lituu mwa mufuse kuli ahapelezwe kuina ni kuanopa hape. Manzibuana Hase asebelize ni kuboteha ile naasina mumbeta fa kulobala kono akengama feela kwa liiso ni kulobala mwa mufuse mi bamubiza Sindelela.

text.S1: It happened that the father was once going to the fair, and he asked his two step-daughters what he should bring back for them. "Beautiful dresses," said one, "Pearls and jewels," said the second. "And thou, Cinderella," said he, "what wilt thou have?" "Father, break off for me the first branch which knocks against your hat on your way home."
text.S2: It had once happened that their father was going to the fair. He asked his two step-daughters what he should bring back for them. “Beautiful dresses,” said one step-daughter. “Pearls and jewels,” said the second step-daughter. “What of you Cinderella?” the father asked, "what do you want?" “Father, break off for me the first branch which knocks against your hat as you return home.”
text.T1: Kwaezahala kuli bo ndataabona nebaya kwa poniso ya lika zeshutana-shutana, mi kacwalo, babuza bana babona bawo ba basizani bamwenda kumongo zewo neba tabela kuli baba lekele haba kuta. “Mandelesi amande,” kwabulela musizana wapili. “Masale ni maseka," kwabulela musizana wabubeli. “Wena bo, Sindelela?” bamubuza. “Nikushimbele likamañi?” “Tate, na munilobele mutai wa kota yapili yeka ngungula kwa kuwani yamina hamunze mukutela kwa hae.”

text.S1: So he bought beautiful dresses, pearls and jewels for his two step-daughters, and on his return home, as he was riding through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and knocked off his hat. Then he broke off the branch and took it with him. When he reached home he gave his step-daughters the things which they had wished for, and to Cinderella he gave the branch from the hazel-bush. Cinderella thanked him, went to her mother's grave and planted the branch on it, and wept so much that the tears fell down on it and watered it.
text.S2: So he bought beautiful dresses, pearls and jewels for his two step-daughters, and on his return home, as he was riding through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and knocked off his hat. Then he plucked the branch and carried it with him. When he reached home he gave his step-daughters the things which they had wished to be brought. As for Cinderella, he was given the branch from the hazel-bush. Cinderella thanked him, went to her mother's grave and planted the branch on it. She wept so much that the tears that fell down on it watered it.
text.T1: Cwale baleka mandelesi amande, masale ni maseka a bana bahae ba basizana bamwenda kumongo. Mwa nzila ya kukutela kwa hae inge basweli kucoba njinga cwalo mwa macecani amatala atibani hahulu, mutai wa kota ya hazelu wangunyuta kwa kuwani yabona ni kuiwiseza fafasi. Baloba mutai wone uwisize kuwani ni kuushimba. Habafita kwa hae bafa bana babona ba basizana bamwenda kumongo lika zene babalaezize. Haili yena Sindelela afiwa mutai wa kota ya hezelu yanaa laezize. Sindelela aitumela hahulu ku bo ndatahe mi aliba ni mutai woo kwa libita la bo mahe ni kuyo ucala fateñi. Hase afelize kucala mutai woo fa libita, alila hahulu kuli ni mioko yahae yalotela fa libita ni kuselaela mutai woo.

text.S1: And it grew, however, and became a handsome tree. Twice a day Cinderella went and sat beneath it, and wept and prayed, and a little white bird always came on the tree, and if Cinderella expressed a wish, the bird would throw down to her what she had wished for.
text.S2: The tree branch that was planted on the grave became a good tree. Twice a day Cinderella used to visit the mother’s grave and sat under the tree where she wept and prayed. In the process, a little white bird was seen landing on the same tree, and if Cinderella expressed her wish, the bird would throw it down to her.
text.T1: Mutai wahula ni kuba kota yende. Habeli ka zazi, Sindelela ayaanga kuyoina mwatasaa kota yewo alila ni kulapela. Zewo hali ezahala, kanyunywani kakasweu nekanze kalulanga fa kota yewo, mi haiba Sindelela abulela takazo yahae neka muyumbela yona mwataasi.

text.S1: It happened, however, that the King appointed a festival which was to last three days, and to which all the beautiful young girls in the country were invited. When the two stepsisters heard that they too were to appear among the number, they were delighted, called Cinderella and said, "Comb our hair for us, brush our shoes and fasten our buckles, for we are going to the festival at the King's palace." Cinderella obeyed, but wept because she too would have liked to go to the dance, and begged her step-mother to allow her to do so.
text.S2: It happened, that the King organised a festival which would last three days, at which all beautiful young girls in the country were invited to attend. When the two step-sisters heard that they too were to appear among the number, they were excited. They asked Cinderella and said, “Comb our hair, brush our pairs of shoes and fasten our buckles, because we are going to the festival at the King's palace.” Cinderella obeyed their instructions, but wept because she too would have liked to go to the dance. She therefore, requested her step-mother for permission to allow her also to go to the palace.
text.T1: Kwaezahala kuli Mulena alukisa mukiti wone ukaanga mazazi amalaalu, ili woo basizana babande kaufela mwa naha neba memilwe kubateñi. Basizana bamwenda kumongo habato utwa kuli ni bona neba memilwe kwa mukiti woo mwahalaa babañwi batabela hahulu. Babiza Sindelela ni kumubulela bali, “Lukamune milili yaluna, lupolisheze makatulo aluna ni kulutama makanda, kakuli luya kwa mukiti wa mulena kwa Kwandu.” Sindelela alatelela taelo yewo kono nihakulicwalo, alila kakuli niyena naana ni takazo ya kuya kwa mukiti wa kubina woo. Mi akupa bo mahe bamutose kuli bamu lumeleze kuya kwateñi.

text.S1: "Thou go, Cinderella!" said she; "Thou art dusty and dirty and wouldst go to the festival? Thou hast no clothes and shoes, and yet wouldst dance!" As, however, Cinderella went on asking, the step-mother at last said, "I have emptied a dish of lentils into the ashes for thee, if thou hast picked them out again in two hours, thou shalt go with us." The maiden went through the back-door into the garden, and called, "You tame pigeons, you turtle-doves, and all you birds beneath the sky, come and help me to pick the good into the pot, the bad into the crop."
text.S2: “Cinderella do you also wish to attend?” asked the step-mother, “Dusty and dirty as you are, wish to attend the festival? Without good clothes and shoes, and yet you want to dance!” Cinderella kept on asking for permission from the step-mother who finally said, “I have emptied a dish of lentils into the ashes for you, if case you quickly picked them again in two hours, then you would join us.” The maiden went through the back-door into the garden and called, “You tame pigeons! You turtle-doves! Also all of you birds beneath the sky! Come and help me to pick the good into the pot, the bad into the crop.”
text.T1: “Sindelela ni wena ubata kuya!” bo mahe bamutose bamu bulelela. “Wena yainzi mwa maluli ni masila ubata kuya kwa mukiti? Hauna litino ni makatulo, mi ubata kuyobina!” Sindelela atundamena kukupa bo mahe bamutose kuli baye ni yena, mi bona bali, “Nisululezi muloho wone uli mwa sikotolo mwa mufuse waaka mi haiba ukakona kuunopa mwa lihola zepeli, kipeto ukaya niluna.” Musizana azwela kwa munyako wa kwa mulaho wa ndu, wone uzwela mwa simu ya miloho ni kuyohuwa ali, “Mina tunkwilimba, mina maiba ni mina linyunywani kaufela zemwatasaa lihalimu, hamutahe mutoni tusa kunopa zende kulibeya mwa poto mi zemaswe kubeya mwa kutulo.”

text.S1: Then two white pigeons came in by the kitchen-window, and afterwards the turtle-doves, and at last all the birds beneath the sky, came whirring and crowding in, and alighted amongst the ashes. And the pigeons nodded with their heads and began to pick, pick, pick, pick, and the rest also began to pick, pick, pick, pick, and gathered all the good grains into the dish. Hardly had one hour passed before they had finished, and all flew out again. Then the girl took the dish to her step-mother, and was glad, and believed that now she would be allowed to go with them to the festival. But the step-mother said, "No, Cinderella, thou hast no clothes and thou canst not dance; thou wouldst only be laughed at."

Cinderella you won’t go because you do not have good clothes for the dance and as such people will only laugh at you.”
text.T1: Cwaie tunkwilimba totubeli twataha kakukenela mwa lihaulo la situngu, mi kasamulaho maiba ni linyunywani kaufela zamwatasaa lihalimu zataha inge kakundukundu, kutobundama ni kulula fa mufuse. Tunkwilimba twainamisa litoho ni kukalisa kunopaka- nopaka bubeke, mi ni linyunywani zeñwi kaufela zakalisa kunopaka-nopaka cwalo bubeke bobunde ni kububeya mwa sikotolo. Hakusika fita nihaiba hola iliñwi zafeza ni kufufa hape kuya. Cwale musizana aanga sikotolo ni kusiisa ku bo mahe bamutose ka tabo, ni kusepa kuli cwale naaka lumelezwa kuya ni bona kwa mukiti. Kono bo mahe bamutose bali, “Awa wena Sindelela, hauna litino mi haukoni kuyobina kakuli ukayo sehiwa feela.”

And she thought to herself, "That she most certainly cannot do." When the step-mother had emptied the two dishes of lentils amongst the ashes, the maiden went through the back-door into the garden and cried, You tame pigeons, you turtle-doves, and all you birds under heaven, come and help me to pick the good into the pot, The bad into the crop."

And the doves nodded with their heads and began to pick, pick, pick, pick, and the others began also pick, pick, pick, pick, and gathered all the good seeds into the dishes, and before half an hour was over they had already finished, and all flew out again. Then the maid- en carried the dishes to the step-mother and was delighted, and believed that she might now go with them to the festival. But the step-mother said, "All this will not help thee; thou goest not with us, for thou hast no clothes and canst not dance; we should be ashamed of thee!" On this she turned her back on Cinderella, and hurried away with her two proud daughters.

Then the bird threw a gold and silver dress down to her, and slippers embroidered with silk and silver. She put on the dress with all speed, and went to the festival. Her step-sisters and the step-mother however did not know her, and thought she must be a foreign princess, for she looked so beautiful in the golden dress.

text.S1: They never once thought of Cinderella, and believed that she was sitting at home in the dirt, picking lentils out of the ashes. The prince went to meet her, took her by the hand and danced with her. He would dance with no other maiden, and never let loose of her hand, and if anyone else came to invite her, he said, "This is my partner.” She danced till it was evening, and then she wanted to go home. But the King's son said, "I will go with thee and bear thee company," for he wished to see to whom the beautiful maiden belonged. She escaped from him, however, and sprang into the pigeon-house. The King's son waited until her father came, and then he told him that the stranger maiden had leapt into the pigeon-house.

Nabi nasalati kubina ni musizana usili kwandaa yena feela. Hape na salati kutuhela lizoho lahae. Haiba nji mutu usili amutela kutokupa kubina ni yena, Nabi naali, “Yo ki mulikanaaka.” Musizana abina lizazi kaufela konji kuyoli likelisa ka nako yewo nabata kukuta kwa hae. Kono Nabi ali, “Nikaya ni wena kuli nikusindekete.” Nabi sanaa bata ki kubona lapa lanaa pila musizana yomunde cwalo. Nihakulicwalo, musizana apicuka Nabi ni kuyo ipata mwa sitantwe sa tunkwilimba. text.S1: The old man thought, "Can it be Cinderella?" and they had to bring him an axe and a pickaxe that he might hew the pigeon-house to pieces, but no one was inside it. And when they got home Cinderella lay in her dirty clothes among the ashes, and a dim little oil-lamp was burning on the mantle-piece, for Cinderella had jumped quickly down from the back of the pigeon-house and had run to the little hazel-tree, and there she had taken off her beautiful clothes and laid them on the grave, and the bird had taken them away again, and then she had placed herself in the kitchen amongst the ashes in her gray gown.

text.S1: Next day when the festival began afresh, and her parents and the step- sisters had gone once more, Cinderella went to the hazel-tree and said "Shiver and quiver, my little tree, silver and gold throw down over me." Then the bird threw down a much more beautiful dress than on the preceding day. And when Cinderella appeared at the festival in this dress, everyone was astonished at her beauty. The King's son had waited until she came, and instantly took her by the hand and danced with no one but her. When others came and invited her, he said, "She is my partner." When evening came she wished to leave, and the King's son followed her and wanted to see which house she went to. But she sprang away from him, and into the garden behind the house.

text.S1: Therein stood a beautiful tall tree on which hung the most magnificent pears. She clambered so nimbly between the branches like a squirrel that the King's son did not know where she was gone. text.S1: When evening came, Cinderella wished to leave, and the King's son was anxious to go with her, but she escaped from him so quickly that he could not follow her. The King's son had, however, used a stratagem, and had caused the whole staircase to be smeared with pitch, and there, when she ran down, had the maiden's left slipper remained sticking. text.S1: When the wedding with the King's son had to be celebrated, the two false sisters came and wanted to get into favor with Cinderella and share her good fortune.
